HARD FORMAT RULES (verify against the compiler; the compiler wins)
Files:
- `content/books/<slug>/book.yml`: `title`, `author`, `summary`, `date`, `tags`, `draft: false`.
- Chapter folders `NN-chapter-slug/` containing `chapter.yml` (`title`, `summary`, `draft: false`).
- Section files `NN-subchapter-slug.md` inside chapter folders. Names use lowercase letters, digits, and single hyphens only.
Front matter of every section: `title` and `questions` (5–7 questions).
Each question has: `id`, `prompt`, `type`, `explanation`, `options`.
- `id`: unique lowercase slug within the section (letters, digits, hyphens). NEVER `yes`, `no`, `true`, `false`, `null` (any case).
- `type`: ALWAYS present, either `single` (exactly 1 correct option) or `multiple` (2–3 correct options out of 5; the prompt must end with "Select all that apply.").
- `options`: 4–5 items; each has `text`; right answers also have `correct: true`; wrong answers have no `correct` key.
- `explanation`: required on every question and fully self-contained. Structure: (a) why the correct option(s) hold, with the rule or standard behind it; (b) why EACH distractor fails, naming the specific misconception; (c) every query result, truth table, index lookup, or interleaved schedule traced step by step. Refer to options by their text, NEVER by letter or position (e.g., never "option B").
YAML safety:
- Double-quote every string value (`title`, `id`, `prompt`, option `text`, `summary`, etc.). Escape inner double quotes. This avoids boolean/number/null coercion and `: ` / ` #` / leading `` ` `` `@` `[` `{` `*` `- ` problems (e.g., the option text `"NULL"`, `"UNKNOWN"`, `"0"`).
- Long explanations: use a block scalar (`explanation: |-` with indented lines) if the compiler or existing books accept it; otherwise a double-quoted string. Test with the real compiler on the first section before writing the rest.
- Never put `---` at the start of a line inside front matter content.
Markdown body:
- The body starts with `## Learning objectives` (3–5 bullets), then the structure below.
- Every fenced code block has a language tag from this set, intersected with what `SyntaxHighlighter` supports: `csharp`, `python`, `javascript`, `sql`, `bash`, `json`, `yaml`, `html`. Use Markdown tables for sample relations, result sets, truth tables, and interleaved transaction schedules. Keep snippets short and exact.
Answer-position balance (the UI does not shuffle): for question number k (1-based) in section number s of the book, place the first correct option at index ((k + s) mod n), 0-based, where n is that question's option count; for `multiple` questions, place correct options at that index and the next valid index(es). validate.py must verify that no position holds more than 40% of the correct answers within any section.

SECTION STRUCTURE (400–1200 words of prose per section, one crisp concept each)
1. `## Learning objectives`
2. `## The invariant` : the timeless mechanism, stated precisely, with the primary-source rule behind it.
3. `## Worked example` : concrete sample data, a trace, or a short code sample with exact expected output.
4. `## Where this shows up today` : the relevance block (see policy below).
5. `## Pitfalls checklist` : 3–6 bullets of mistakes engineers actually make.
6. `## Key takeaways` : 3–5 bullets.

TIMELESS-VS-CURRENT POLICY (apply strictly)
- At most ONE question per section may depend on a fact that could change within five years (a default setting, a version-specific feature). All other questions must rest on invariants: relational algebra, logic, ISO SQL semantics, algorithmic limits, anomaly definitions.
- The "Where this shows up today" block is at most about 15% of the section. It connects the invariant to how the world looks in 2026: current engines, current defaults, current practice. Every dated claim must be written as "As of November 2026, ..." and, if it names an engine, version, or default, include the version. Name products only as examples of a mechanism, never as the point.
- If web access is available, verify every dated claim, version, default isolation level, and feature (for example, newer SQL standard features, engine-specific behavior) against official documentation (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, SQLite, vendor docs) before writing it. If you cannot verify a current-state claim, drop it or restate it as a general mechanism. Never guess versions, dates, or adoption figures.
- Citations: cite sources at document level (Codd 1970; ISO/IEC 9075; Berenson et al. 1995; Cahill, Röhm and Fekete 2008; Fekete et al. 2005; official engine docs); add a section or page number only when you have confirmed it. Never fabricate a quote or reference. ALWAYS separate three layers explicitly: (1) what the ANSI/ISO standard says, (2) what the theory says, (3) what a specific engine actually does.
- Dated facts must never be the only reason an answer is correct.

QUESTION QUALITY RULES
- Mix per section: at least 2 compute-or-trace questions (query output, row counts, index choice, schedule outcome), at least 1 "spot the bug / what does this query return" question, and the rest conceptual or scenario-based.
- Distractors are real misconceptions, plausible and parallel in length and style; the correct option must not be systematically the longest.
- No "all of the above" or "none of the above". No trick wording. No negations in stems unless emphasized with NOT.
- Every question must be answerable using only what that section teaches plus the explanation. No concept is tested twice across the whole book except in Chapter 7 (review), which must combine concepts from earlier chapters.
- Prompts are Markdown; use inline code for identifiers and values. Sample data for questions should be small enough (≤ 8 rows) to trace by hand.

EXEMPLAR (shape only; do not copy its content)
````markdown
---
title: "Integer Division Truncation"
questions:
  - id: "negative-division"
    type: "single"
    prompt: "In C#, what does `-7 / 2` evaluate to?"
    explanation: |-
      C# integer division truncates toward zero, so the exact quotient -3.5 becomes -3.
      "-4" is what floor division would give (as in Python's `//`), but C# does not floor.
      "-3.5" is wrong because both operands are `int`, so the result is `int`.
      "4" ignores the sign entirely.
      Arithmetic: 7 / 2 = 3 remainder 1, so |quotient| = 3; the sign is negative, giving -3.
    options:
      - text: "-4"
      - text: "-3"
        correct: true
      - text: "-3.5"
      - text: "4"
---

## Learning objectives

- Predict the result of integer division for negative operands.

## The invariant

...
````

BOOK SPECIFICATION
- Slug: relational-sql-and-transactions
- Title: "Relational Theory, SQL Semantics & Transaction Anomalies"
- Summary: "The timeless mechanics of relational algebra, SQL's logical execution and three-valued logic, B-tree indexing invariants, and MVCC/lock-based transaction isolation levels."
- Tags: [sql, databases, relational-theory, transactions, concurrency]
- Author/date: author id per Step 0; `date` = 2026-11-27 in the repo's date format.
- Audience: working software engineers who write SQL but have never studied the theory. Prerequisites: basic SELECT/JOIN/GROUP BY, general programming. Prefer portable SQL; mark any dialect-specific syntax clearly with the engine name.
- Primary sources to cite where relevant: E.F. Codd (1970); ISO/IEC 9075 (SQL standard); Berenson et al. (1995) "A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels"; Fekete et al. (2005) and Cahill, Röhm, Fekete (2008) on snapshot isolation and SSI; Comer (1979) "The Ubiquitous B-Tree"; official PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, SQL Server, and SQLite documentation.

Chapters (folder names fixed; choose 3–5 sections for each):
01-relational-foundations-and-normalization: sets vs SQL multisets (bags), superkeys, candidate, primary and foreign keys, functional dependencies, 1NF/2NF/3NF/BCNF with concrete insert, update, and delete anomalies on small tables, lossless decomposition, when controlled denormalization is justified. Today: JSON/document columns in relational engines as a deliberate 1NF trade-off; analytics-oriented denormalized models.
02-sql-logical-query-processing-order: FROM -> JOIN/ON -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT/OFFSET; why aliases work in ORDER BY but not in WHERE/HAVING (and the dialect exceptions); WHERE vs ON in LEFT OUTER JOIN; EXISTS vs IN vs JOIN and duplicate-multiplication traps; logical order vs physical execution order (the optimizer may reorder if the result is equivalent). Today: CTEs and whether engines inline or materialize them (verify per engine and version).
03-three-valued-logic-and-null-semantics: TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN truth tables for AND, OR, NOT; why `WHERE x <> 5` drops NULL rows; why `NOT IN (subquery)` returns nothing when the subquery yields a NULL while `NOT EXISTS` does not; COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) vs SUM(col) on empty and all-NULL groups; `IS DISTINCT FROM`; NULLs in UNIQUE constraints, GROUP BY, DISTINCT, and ORDER BY across dialects. Today: `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` and engine differences (verify versions).
04-grouping-aggregation-and-window-functions: GROUP BY functional-dependency rule, HAVING vs WHERE, aggregate edge cases, window frames (ROWS vs RANGE vs GROUPS) and the default frame trap, ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK, running totals, top-N per group, gaps and islands. Today: window functions as the standard tool for analytics queries; availability across engines (verify).
05-b-plus-tree-indexes-selectivity-and-joins: B+tree anatomy (fanout, depth arithmetic, linked leaves), composite indexes and the leftmost-prefix rule, sargability (functions on indexed columns, leading wildcards, implicit type conversions), covering indexes and index-only scans, selectivity and the point where a full scan beats an index, nested-loop vs hash vs merge join and when each wins, statistics and cardinality-estimation errors. Today: why hash and LSM-based indexes, columnar storage, and vector indexes are different structures solving different problems (mechanism-level only; verify any named feature).
06-transaction-anomalies-and-isolation-levels: dirty write, dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update, read skew, write skew with fully worked interleaved schedules; ANSI SQL-92 levels vs Berenson et al.; two-phase locking vs MVCC vs snapshot isolation vs SSI; `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, gap and next-key locks, deadlock formation and detection, retries on serialization failure. Today: default isolation levels and real behavior of REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE in PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, SQL Server, and SQLite (verify each against current docs; state versions); distributed SQL systems that offer serializability.
07-cross-chapter-review-and-debugging: multi-table query-output puzzles, composite-index selection puzzles, and interleaved transaction-schedule anomaly identification that combine earlier chapters.
